weighted_matrix.title: Weighted decision matrix
weighted_matrix.source: Decision matrix. Also called weighted scoring or Pugh matrix.
weighted_matrix.intro: Score each option against the criteria. A criterion with a high weight has more effect on the result.
how: Choose the option that you prefer now. Do this before you score. Your feeling is data.
Give each criterion a weight from 1 to 5.
Give each option a score from 1 to 5 for each criterion.
Read the ranking. Then read the notes below it.
weighted_matrix.readout: The top score is a guide. It is not a verdict. If the score does not match your feeling, a criterion is missing or a weight is wrong. Find which one.

prompts.q: Does a criterion matter to you, but it is not in the table?
Change your most important weight by one step. Does the winner change?
choices: No, the winner stays the same
Yes, the winner changes
I did not test it

eisenhower.title: Eisenhower matrix: urgent or important?
eisenhower.source: Eisenhower matrix. From The Decision Book.
eisenhower.intro: Sort your tasks by importance and urgency. Then act on each group in a different way.
how: Add each task that you must do now.
Put each task in one box.
Do the top-right box first. Plan the top-left box. Give the bottom-right box to another person. Do the bottom-left box later or remove it.
eisenhower.itemPlaceholder: Type a task and press Add

tl.name: Important, not urgent
tl.when: It matters much. The deadline is not near.
tl.action: Decide when to do it. Put it in your calendar.

tr.name: Urgent and important
tr.when: It matters much. Time is short.

bl.name: Not important, not urgent
bl.when: It has little value. Time is not short.
bl.action: Do it later or remove it.

br.name: Urgent, not important
br.when: Time is short. It does not matter much.

eisenhower.readout: If the top-left box is empty, you may work only on urgent tasks. Important tasks that you do not plan often become urgent.

swot.title: SWOT analysis
swot.source: SWOT analysis. From The Decision Book.
swot.intro: Understand the situation before you choose a solution. List what helps and what hurts. Include factors inside and outside your control.

columns.name: Strengths
columns.hint: Inside. What do we do well?

columns.name: Opportunities
columns.hint: Outside. Which chances can we use?

how: Write 3 to 5 items in each box. Be specific.
Then answer the four questions below.

prompts.q: How can we use our strengths more?
How can we reduce our weaknesses?
How can we use the opportunities?
How can we protect ourselves from the threats?

bcg_box.title: BCG box: where to invest?
bcg_box.source: BCG matrix. From The Decision Book.
bcg_box.intro: Sort products, business units, or projects by market growth and by your share of the market.
how: Add each product or unit.
Place each one by market growth (up is fast growth) and by relative market share (right is a bigger share).
Do the action in each box.
bcg_box.itemPlaceholder: Type a product or unit and press Add

tl.name: Question marks
tl.action: This is a hard decision. Invest strongly or stop.

bl.name: Dogs
bl.action: Sell or close it. Keep it only if it has a value that is not financial.

br.name: Cash cows
br.action: Keep it. It costs little and gives a high return.

project_portfolio.title: Project portfolio matrix
project_portfolio.source: Project portfolio matrix. From The Decision Book.
project_portfolio.intro: You can have many projects. Decide which projects to keep, change, give to other people, or stop.
how: List all your projects. Include work projects and private projects.
Place each project by two things. First, how much it helps your main goal. Second, how much you learn from it.
project_portfolio.itemPlaceholder: Type a project and press Add

x.label: How much it helps my main goal

y.label: How much I learn from it

tl.name: Change the project
tl.when: It helps little. You learn much.
tl.action: Change it to serve your main goal. Or keep it as a learning project.

tr.name: Very good project
tr.when: It helps much. You learn much.
tr.action: Protect your time for these projects.

bl.name: Stop the project
bl.when: It helps little. You learn little.

br.name: Give it to another person
br.when: It helps much. You learn little.
br.action: The result matters, but you learn little. Give it to another person if you can.

feedback_box.title: Feedback box
feedback_box.source: Feedback box. From The Decision Book.
feedback_box.intro: Sort the feedback that you received. Decide which feedback to use and which feedback to ignore.
how: Write each piece of feedback as one short line.
Place it by what you think of your work and by what the feedback says.
feedback_box.itemPlaceholder: Type one piece of feedback and press Add

x.label: What I think of my work

tl.name: Suggestion
tl.when: I think it is bad, but I accept it.

tr.name: Compliment
tr.when: I think it is good too. It can stay.

bl.name: Criticism
bl.when: I think it is bad too. It must change.

br.name: Advice
br.when: I think it is good, but it must change.
br.action: Think carefully. Decide which advice to follow.

hard_choice.title: Hard choice model: what kind of decision is this?
hard_choice.source: Hard choice model. From The Decision Book.
hard_choice.intro: Each decision has two traits. The first trait is how easy it is to compare the options. The second trait is the size of the consequences. Place your decision to see how much effort it needs.
how: Add each decision that you have.
Place each decision in the box that fits best.
hard_choice.itemPlaceholder: Type a decision and press Add

tl.name: Easy choice
tl.action: One option is better. A wrong choice costs little. Decide fast.

tr.name: Big but clear
tr.action: The better option is clear. The decision is big, but it is easy.

bl.name: Different options
bl.action: Each option is good in a different way. Follow your preference.

br.name: Hard choice
br.action: No answer is clearly right. Support your choice with strong personal reasons. Use more tools.

rumsfeld.title: Rumsfeld matrix: what do I know about the risks?
rumsfeld.source: Rumsfeld matrix. From The Decision Book.
rumsfeld.intro: Sort what you know and what you do not know about a plan or a risk. The gaps show what to learn.
how: List facts, risks, and worries.
Place each item in a box.
Then ask what you can do about the unknown boxes.
rumsfeld.itemPlaceholder: Type a fact, risk, or worry and press Add

x.label: Awareness
x.high: I do not know about it

tl.name: Known knowns
tl.when: We know it exists. We have a countermeasure.

tr.name: Unknown knowns
tr.when: We have no evidence, but we feel that it exists.

bl.name: Known unknowns
bl.when: We know it exists. We cannot tell when it happens.
bl.action: Make a plan. Set a warning sign.

br.name: Unknown unknowns
br.when: We do not know that we do not know.
br.action: Ask people outside your group. Keep a reserve. Do a pre-mortem.

johari.title: Johari window
johari.source: Johari window. From The Decision Book.
johari.intro: See yourself through four windows. The windows show what you and other people know about you. Use it before a big choice about your career or role.
how: Choose words that describe you, for example reliable or fun. Place each word.
Ask 2 or 3 people to choose words for you. Add their words and place them.
johari.itemPlaceholder: Type a word that describes you and press Add

tl.name: Open
tl.when: I know it. Others know it.

tr.name: Blind spot
tr.when: I do not know it. Others know it.
tr.action: Feedback can help here. It can also hurt.

bl.name: Hidden
bl.when: I know it. I hide it.
bl.action: Ask why you hide it. Share what is safe.

br.name: Unknown
br.when: I do not know it. Others do not know it.
br.action: Sometimes something new appears. Stay curious.

flow_model.title: Flow model: what makes you happy?
flow_model.source: Flow model by Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi. Also in The Decision Book.
flow_model.intro: Place your activities by the challenge that they give and by your ability. Flow happens when the challenge and the ability match.
how: List your main tasks or activities.
Place each one by how hard it is for you and by how skilled you are.
flow_model.itemPlaceholder: Type an activity and press Add

tl.name: Overchallenged
tl.action: You can burn out. Reduce the challenge or learn more skill.

bl.name: Apathy
bl.action: Find something that matters to you.

br.name: Underchallenged
br.action: You can feel bored. Increase the challenge.

flow_model.readout: Flow needs strong focus, a task that you chose, the right challenge, a clear goal, and quick feedback.

force_field.title: Force field analysis
force_field.source: Force field analysis by Kurt Lewin.
force_field.intro: Forces push for a change. Other forces hold it back. The change happens only when the pushing forces are stronger.
how: Write the change that you want in the decision question.
List the driving forces on the left. List the restraining forces on the right.
Give each force a score from 1 to 5.
Make a plan to reduce the strongest restraining force.
force_field.leftWins: The driving forces are stronger. The change can work. Also reduce the biggest restraining force.
force_field.rightWins: The restraining forces are stronger. The change stops unless you reduce them.
force_field.tip: Lewin advised to reduce the restraining forces. Do not only push harder. A change to one force can make new forces. Check again after your first action.

prompts.q: Which restraining force can you reduce? How?
Which driving force can you make stronger? How?

pros_cons.title: Pros and cons with strength scores
pros_cons.source: Pros and cons list with weights.
pros_cons.intro: List reasons for and reasons against. Give each reason a strength score. A small reason then does not count as much as a big reason.
how: List the reasons for on the left. List the reasons against on the right.
Give each reason a score from 1 to 5.
Read the balance. Then read the biggest item on each side.
pros_cons.balanced: The two sides are equal. The totals do not decide. Read the biggest item on each side. Do a pre-mortem.
pros_cons.tip: A list can have bias. Ask a person who does not agree with you to add one item to each side.

rubber_band.title: Rubber band model
rubber_band.source: Rubber band model. From The Decision Book.
rubber_band.intro: Use this tool when you cannot choose between two important options. Write what pulls you and what holds you back. Your feelings can show which way you already lean.
how: Write what pulls you toward the change.
Write what holds you where you are.
Ask for each item: is it a fact or a fear?
rubber_band.leftWins: The pull is stronger. You can be near the point of decision.
rubber_band.rightWins: The hold is stronger. Check if the items that hold you are facts or fears.
rubber_band.balanced: The pull and the hold are equal. Try the 10/10/10 test or a small trial.

prompts.q: Which items on the holding side are facts? Which items are fears?
Imagine that the rubber band breaks today. Which way do you move?

decision_tree_ev.title: Decision tree with expected value
decision_tree_ev.source: Decision tree analysis and expected monetary value.
decision_tree_ev.intro: Use this tool when the results are uncertain. You must be able to estimate the chances and the payoffs. The tool changes guesses to numbers that you can compare.
how: Add each option and its cost.
For each option, list what can happen. Give the chance in percent and the payoff.
The chances must total 100%.
Compare the expected value and the worst case.
decision_tree_ev.readout: Expected value is the average result if you could do the choice many times. If you can choose only one time, the worst case matters as much as the average.

ten_ten_ten.title: 10/10/10 test
ten_ten_ten.source: 10-10-10 from Suzy Welch. Also in The Decision Book.
ten_ten_ten.intro: A strong feeling today can hide what matters later. Check how you feel about each option at three points in time.
how: Write your options.
Rate each option. How do you feel after 10 minutes, after 10 months, and after 10 years?
Find the options that are good at all three points.

horizons.label: 10 minutes after you decide
horizons.help: Your first reaction. Often it is fear or relief.

horizons.label: 10 months after you decide
horizons.help: The practical result of the choice.

horizons.label: 10 years after you decide
horizons.help: The big picture. Does it still matter?

ten_ten_ten.readout: An option that is bad after 10 minutes and good after 10 years is often worth it. An option that is good now and bad later is a trap.

trial_run.title: Three-day trial of each option
trial_run.source: The Jesuit method of Ignatius of Loyola. Also in The Decision Book.
trial_run.intro: If two options feel equal, try each option before you choose. Act for 3 days as if you chose option one. Then do the same for option two.
how: Do the trial for option one. Rate your feeling after each day.
Do the same for option two.
Compare how each trial felt.

horizons.label: After day 2
horizons.help: Is the feeling the same, better, or worse?

horizons.label: After day 3
horizons.help: How do you feel about a final choice of this option?

trial_run.readout: Read the trend and the total. A feeling that gets better each day is a good sign.

premortem.title: Pre-mortem: imagine it failed
premortem.intro: Before you commit, imagine that the decision failed. Work backward from the failure and ask why. This makes it safe to name risks that people do not usually say.

steps.q: It is one year later. The decision gave a bad result. What happened? Write one sentence.
List all reasons for the failure. Write fast. Include causes that you or your team made.
Choose the 3 reasons that are most likely or most damaging. Which reason do you notice too late?
For each of the 3 reasons, write one action that reduces the chance or the damage.
Which early warning sign shows that the plan is failing? Who watches for it?
What is your verdict after this exercise?
choices: Go as planned
Go, with the changes above
Test with a small step first
Stop

premortem.readout: A plan that has only reasons for success is a hope. A risk that you name now costs less to fix than a risk that you find later.

doors.title: One-way or two-way door?
doors.source: Type 1 and Type 2 decisions. From the Amazon shareholder letters of Jeff Bezos.
doors.intro: Most decisions can be undone. Do not treat all decisions as if you cannot undo them. Find which kind of decision you have. Then use the right amount of effort.
how: Answer each question.
Do the action at the end.

start.q: If this goes wrong, how hard is it to return?

options.label: Easy. I can undo it fast and at low cost.
Hard. To undo it costs much time, money, or trust.

q_down.q: Can you change it to a two-way door with a smaller first step?
q_down.help: Ideas: a pilot, a trial period, a smaller first commitment, a clear way to exit. Or decide the test now and the full commitment later.

options.label: Yes, I have a smaller first step that I can undo.
No, it is a true one-way door.

outcome.title: Two-way door: decide fast
outcome.text: Choose a good option when you have about 70% of the information. Do it as a trial. Set a review date. A long analysis costs more than a small mistake here.
next: Use a weighted matrix only if the options are close.

outcome.title: Change it to a two-way door first
outcome.text: Do the pilot or the trial. Make the big decision later with real data.
next: Write which result makes you go further.
Write which result makes you stop.

outcome.title: One-way door: go slowly
outcome.text: Give this decision real effort. Use more than one tool. Ask another person for an opinion. Then commit fully.
next: Set a stop rule before you start.

cynefin.title: Cynefin: what kind of situation is this?
cynefin.intro: Different situations need different ways to decide. Find which kind of situation you have before you choose a tool.
how: Answer the questions.
Read the approach at the end.

start.q: Is something urgent and out of control now?
start.help: Examples: a crisis, an emergency, or a sudden failure.

q2.q: How well can you tell what happens if you take an action?

options.label: Very well. Cause and effect are clear. Anyone can see them.
Well enough, but it needs study or an expert.
Not well. I can learn it only if I try and watch.
I cannot tell which of these is true.

outcome.title: Clear: sense, categorize, respond
outcome.text: See the facts. Match them to a known category. Follow the standard method.
next: Use a checklist or a simple rule.

outcome.title: Complicated: sense, analyze, respond
outcome.text: Collect the facts. Ask experts. Compare the options. Then decide.

outcome.title: Complex: probe, sense, respond
outcome.text: You cannot know the result before you act. Run small experiments that are safe to fail. Watch what happens. Do more of what works.
next: Plan small trials. Do not make one big bet.
Do a pre-mortem for each experiment.

outcome.title: Chaotic: act, sense, respond
outcome.text: Take an action to stabilize the situation first. Then see what happened. Move toward a calm situation where you can think.

outcome.title: Not sure: split the problem
outcome.text: Split the problem into smaller parts. Answer these questions for each part. Different parts can be in different situations.
next: Do this check for each part.

yes_no_rule.title: Yes/no rule: decide fast by elimination
yes_no_rule.source: The yes/no rule. From The Decision Book.
yes_no_rule.intro: Use a short chain of yes/no questions to decide fast.
yes_no_rule.authorNote: Write new nodes for the real problem before you build. Use 3 to 5 questions. Every path must end in an outcome.
how: Answer each question with yes or no.
Follow the chain to the result.

q1.q: Replace: Does this need action now?

q2.q: Replace: Can you undo the action?

outcome.title: Wait
outcome.text: Do not act now. Set a date to check again.

outcome.title: Go
outcome.text: Act now. Then review the result.

hersey_blanchard.title: Hersey-Blanchard: how do I lead this person?
hersey_blanchard.source: Hersey-Blanchard situational leadership. From The Decision Book.
hersey_blanchard.intro: The best leadership style depends on the person and the task. Find how ready the person is for this task.
how: Think of one person and one task.
Choose the description that fits the person best for this task.

start.q: How ready is this person for this task?

options.label: New to it: low skill, high enthusiasm.
Learning: some skill, but doubt or stress.
Skilled, but motivation or confidence changes often.

outcome.title: Instruct
outcome.text: Give clear orders and steps. Check often.
next: Show how to do the task.

outcome.title: Coach
outcome.text: Explain why. Ask questions. Help the person find the answer.
next: Ask: what do you think we must do?

outcome.title: Support
outcome.text: Share decisions. Listen. Build confidence. Ask what makes the motivation higher or lower.
next: Ask how the person feels about the task.
Let the person decide how. You agree on what.

outcome.title: Delegate
outcome.text: Give the person projects. Let the person lead. Stay available.
next: Agree on the goal and the deadline.

stop_rule.title: Stop rule: decide when you quit
stop_rule.source: Stop rule. From The Decision Book.
stop_rule.intro: Set your stop rule before you start, while you are calm. In the heat of the moment, it is hard to return. The rule does not change. It saves you from long and painful debates.

steps.q: What is the goal?
What is your fixed limit? Complete this sentence: If we pass ___ without ___, we stop.
steps.help: Use a time, a cost, or a safety limit. Use a clear number or date.

steps.q: What is your flexible limit? It can move if a clear condition is true.
steps.help: Example: if the heart rate is below 150 at 2 pm, we can climb until 3 pm.

steps.q: Who calls the stop? Can another person overrule this person?
What do you do when you reach the limit?
Check your rule.
items: I wrote the limits before the start.
No person can change the fixed limit under pressure.

stop_rule.readout: A stop rule works because it does not change. People broke a rule of this type on Mount Everest in 1996. Eight people died.

buyers_model.title: Buyer's decision model
buyers_model.source: Buyer's decision model. From The Decision Book.
buyers_model.intro: Use this tool when you buy a product or a service and you cannot decide. Examples: a car, a laptop, a vendor.

steps.q: How much research is enough? Set your own limits.
steps.help: Example: search for 3 hours, ask 3 friends, visit 2 shops.

steps.q: List your 5 most important criteria in order.
Remove the last two. Which two did you remove?
How will you feel about this purchase after 10 days, after 10 months, and after 10 years?
Choose a way to decide between equal options.
choices: Let the seller or a friend choose
Flip a coin and notice your feeling
Try each option for 3 days
The options are not equal. I do not need a tie-break.

buyers_model.readout: You never know enough, but you can quickly know too much. Limits stop an endless search.

unconscious_thinking.title: Let your unconscious mind help
unconscious_thinking.source: Theory of unconscious thinking. From The Decision Book.
unconscious_thinking.intro: Use this tool for a complex choice with no clear answer. Take a break from thinking. Your unconscious mind can sort much information. A coin toss can show what you want.

steps.q: Write the key facts and your top 2 options.
Take a real break. Walk, sleep, or do other work.
steps.label: I took a break.

steps.q: Flip the coin. Before it lands, notice what you hope for.
What did you hope for? Is this your answer?

unconscious_thinking.readout: The coin does not decide. Your reaction to the coin decides.

decide_when.title: When do I decide?
decide_when.source: Consequences model. From The Decision Book.
decide_when.intro: No decision is also a decision. At the start of a project you know little, but your choices matter much. Later you know more, but your choices matter less. Decide with enough information. Do not decide too early or too late.

steps.q: What do you know now? What do you not know?
How big are the consequences if you choose wrong?
How much of the information that you need do you have?
What is the latest date when waiting is safe? What does waiting cost?
What do you do?
choices: Decide now
Get one specific piece of information. Then decide by the date.
Decide on the date, even if the information is not complete

rules.then: The consequences are small. Decide now. Waiting costs more than a small mistake.
You know enough. More research gives little.
The stakes are high and you have little information. Find the one or two facts that matter most. Set a firm deadline.

decide_when.readout: If you decide to decide later, tell the people involved. If you do not tell them, they see no decision.

goal_check.title: Goal check: is this the right goal?
goal_check.source: John Whitmore, Coaching for Performance. Also in The Decision Book.
goal_check.intro: Split your goal in two parts. The final goal is the result that you want. The performance goal is what you do and control. Then test the goal.

steps.q: My final goal (what I want at the end):
My performance goal (what I do and control):
SMART check
PURE check
items: Positive (says what I want and not what I avoid)

steps.q: CLEAR check
items: Environmentally sound (fits my life and the people around me)

goal_check.readout: Whitmore calls the third set CLEAR. If a box is empty, rewrite the goal until all boxes are full.

grow.title: GROW: Goal, Reality, Options, Will
grow.source: GROW model by Sir John Whitmore.
grow.intro: GROW has four steps. Use it to think about a personal or work problem. Answer one question at a time.

steps.q: What do I want? What is a good result?
What happens now? What did I try?
What stops me?
What can I do? List at least 3 ideas. Odd ideas are good.
What will I do? When? Who helps me or checks my work?
How committed am I to this step?

rules.then: Your commitment is low. Make the step smaller or change the plan until you feel sure.

regret_minimization.title: Regret minimization
regret_minimization.source: Regret minimization framework by Jeff Bezos.
regret_minimization.intro: Use this tool for a rare and big personal choice. Imagine that you are 80 years old and you look back. Which choice do you regret more?

steps.q: You are 80. You look back at this moment. What do you say to the person that you are now?
How much do you regret that you did NOT do it?
How much do you regret that you did it and failed?

rules.then: Not trying hurts more than failing. This points to a decision to do it. Check it with a pre-mortem.
Failing hurts more than not trying. Find a safer and smaller version.

regret_minimization.readout: Use this tool for rare, personal, big choices. Do not use it for small daily decisions. Do not use it if the safety of other people depends on your choice.

wrap.title: WRAP: four steps to a better choice
wrap.source: WRAP process by Chip and Dan Heath, from the book Decisive.
wrap.intro: WRAP has four steps. The steps help you avoid four common traps: narrow thinking, bias to confirm, short-term emotion, and too much confidence.

steps.q: List all options. Can you do both options (an AND option) and not only one?
Vanishing options test: all your current options disappear. What do you do?
Which person solved a similar problem? What did this person do?
What must be true for your favorite option to work?
Ask a person who does not agree with you: which evidence proves you wrong?
Can you do a small test before you commit?
What do you tell a good friend to do? What does your successor do?
Which of your core values does each option follow?
Imagine that the plan failed. What are the likely reasons?
Set a tripwire. Which sign makes you think again? By which date?

bias_check.title: Bias check: four common thinking mistakes
bias_check.source: Cognitive bias. From The Decision Book.
bias_check.intro: You cannot remove these biases. You can improve your thinking. Check your decision against each bias.

steps.q: What is the first number or fact that you heard? Does it hold you?
Do not trust first impressions.
steps.label: I found a second, independent reference.

steps.q: Which evidence changes your mind? Did you look for it?
Assume that you are wrong.
steps.label: I asked a person who does not agree.

steps.q: Do you use one story that you remember and not real data?
Do not trust stories.
steps.label: I checked a larger sample or real numbers.

steps.q: Which part of your decision was a quick feeling?
steps.help: Test: a coffee and a cookie cost $1.10 together. The coffee costs $1 more than the cookie. How much is the cookie? Most people say 10 cents. The right answer is 5 cents.

steps.q: Read it again before you send it.
steps.label: I read my decision again or waited one night.

personal_performance.title: Personal performance model: do I change my job?
personal_performance.source: Personal performance model from The Decision Book. This version starts from a shared purpose.
personal_performance.intro: Look at your role with three questions. What do others expect from you? What can you do? What do you want? Start from the purpose of the work, not only from yourself.

steps.q: What is the purpose of your work or role?
Have to: how much do others expect from you to reach this purpose?
Able to: how well can you do what others expect?
Want to: how much of this work matches what you really want?

rules.then: You can do the work, but you do not want it. Find a different role, or a different meaning in this role.
You want it, but you cannot do it yet. Learn skills or get support.
The fit is weak on both. Think seriously about a change of role.
The fit is good. Check the expectations. Are they too low or too high?

personal_performance.readout: The original model starts only from the person. This version starts from the purpose of the work. Your choice then stays connected to the people and goals that you serve.

six_hats.title: Six thinking hats
six_hats.source: Six thinking hats by Edward de Bono. Also in The Decision Book.
six_hats.intro: Look at the problem in six ways, one way at a time. A moderator must make sure that everyone uses the same hat at the same time.

steps.q: What is the big picture? What is the goal of this discussion?
What are the facts? What do we know? What do we not know?
What are my feelings and first reactions? You do not need to explain them.
What can go wrong? Where is the weak point?
What is the best case? What is good about it?
Which new ideas or options can we find?
What did we learn? What is our next step?

six_hats.readout: A team of the same type of people thinks in the same way. Mix the roles.

appreciative_inquiry.title: Appreciative inquiry: develop ideas
appreciative_inquiry.source: Appreciative inquiry 4-D model. From The Decision Book.
appreciative_inquiry.intro: Focus on strengths and potential. Take an idea that is not complete. Continue to develop it. Do not drop it too early.

steps.q: When a person shares an idea, how do you usually react?
choices: 'No!' (the dictator)
'The idea is good, but...' (the fault-finder)
'No, the idea is not good because...' (the school teacher)
'Yes, and we can also...' (the appreciative thinker)

steps.q: What gives life? What is the best part of what exists now?
What can be? Imagine what is possible.
What must be? Build the ideal together.
What will be? How do we do it well?

team_performance.title: Team performance model
team_performance.source: Drexler/Sibbet team performance model. From The Decision Book.
team_performance.intro: Change a group to a team. Ask each member to rate each stage. Work on the first stage that is not resolved.

steps.q: Orientation: Why am I here?
Trust building: Who are you?
Goal clarification: What are we doing?
Commitment: How will we do it?
Implementation: Who does what, when, and where?
High performance: Wow!
Renewal: Why continue?

rules.then: Orientation is weak. Make the purpose clear. Make clear who is in the team. Signs: disorientation, uncertainty, fear.
Trust is weak. Make time to know each other. Signs: caution, mistrust, a false front.
The goals are not clear. Make the goals clear and shared. Signs: apathy, doubt, competition that does not help.
Commitment is weak. Assign roles and resources. Make decisions. Signs: dependence, resistance, conflict.
Implementation is weak. Make the process clear. Signs: missed deadlines, overload.
Renewal is weak. Recognize and celebrate the results. Signs: boredom, burnout.

swiss_cheese.title: Swiss cheese model: how mistakes happen
swiss_cheese.source: Swiss cheese model. From The Decision Book.
swiss_cheese.intro: A mistake usually happens when holes in many layers of defense line up. Find the holes before they line up.

steps.q: What went wrong, or what can go wrong?
What kind of mistake is it?
choices: Real mistake (a person used the wrong process)
Black-out (a person forgot a step)
Slip-up (a person used the right process in a wrong way)

steps.q: People: which people take part (boss, team, colleagues)? What goes wrong between them?
Technical: which equipment or workplace problems cause the mistake?
Organization: which task or timing problems cause the mistake?
Outside influences: time, economy, mood, weather?
Which check, process, or timing change closes the holes?
How do you respond if the worst event still happens?

double_loop.title: Double-loop learning
double_loop.source: Double-loop learning. From The Decision Book.
double_loop.intro: Learn from mistakes on two levels. In the single loop, you change your actions. In the double loop, you question the goals and beliefs behind your actions.

steps.q: What did you do? What was the result?
What result did you expect?
Single loop: which action can you change?
Double loop: which goal, value, or belief made you act this way?
What do you do if this belief is not true?

making_of.title: Making-of model: understand your past
making_of.source: Making-of model. From The Decision Book.
making_of.intro: To decide your future, first understand your past. Choose a time period. List the facts of what happened.
making_of.promptsTitle: Build the bridge to the future

prompts.q: Which things from the past do you take into the future? Which things do you leave behind?

gap_in_market.title: Gap-in-the-market model
gap_in_market.source: Gap-in-the-market model. From The Decision Book.
gap_in_market.intro: Look at the market on several dimensions at one time. Find a gap that no company fills.

steps.q: Choose 3 dimensions, for example price, location, and how popular or cool it is.
List the competitors. Rate each competitor on the three dimensions (0 to 10).
Where is the market crowded? Can you become the clear leader there?
Where is a gap that other companies do not see?
Is there real demand in that gap? An empty space can mean that nobody wants it. How do you check?

morphological_box.title: Morphological box and SCAMPER
morphological_box.source: Morphological box and SCAMPER. From The Decision Book.
morphological_box.intro: Use a structure to be creative. Split the problem into parts. List options for each part. Then combine one option from each part in new ways.

columns.name: Part 1
columns.hint: Write the name of the part, then the options

morphological_box.promptsTitle: Combine the options and extend the ideas

prompts.q: Choose one option from each part. Write 2 or 3 combinations that can work.
SCAMPER. Substitute: what can you replace?
Combine: what can you join together?
Adapt: what can you take from another area?
Modify: what can you make bigger, smaller, or different?
Put to other use: who else can use this?
Reverse: what happens if you do it the other way?

maslow_check.title: Maslow pyramid: what do I need and what do I want?
maslow_check.source: Hierarchy of needs by Abraham Maslow. Also in The Decision Book.
maslow_check.intro: Needs and wants are different. Check which needs you meet today. Basic needs come first.

steps.q: Physical needs (food, sleep, warmth): how well do you meet them?
Security (home, job, health, protection): how well do you meet it?
Social relationships (friends, partner, love): how well do you meet them?
Recognition (status, respect, money): how well do you meet it?
Self-actualization (to become who you can be): how well do you meet it?
What do you want that is not a need?

rules.then: Meet your basic needs first: food, sleep, warmth.
Security is the lowest need that you do not meet. Be careful with risky choices that put it in danger.
Relationships are the lowest need that you do not meet. A choice that hurts your relationships can cost more than it gives.
